title: Benq’s 4K Home Projector Is a Gamer’s Delight
gist: A 6/10 review of the BenQ TK705STi short-throw 4K projector (about $1,599–$1,698), recommended narrowly to gamers for its low-latency ALLM mode and placement flexibility, but judged merely average for movies and TV due to weak contrast, flat color, and poor daytime viewing. The reviewer also hit finicky auto-keystoning and a known Google TV QR-code setup glitch.

themes.theme: Segmenting by use case, not price

insights.claim: The BenQ TK705STi is worth buying specifically for gamers who want low latency and a large screen and who do not need high-end home-cinema picture quality, since its overall performance is just average.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Midrange projectors now differentiate on latency for gaming rather than cinema fidelity — a category repositioning worth tracking in display demand.
insights.quote: Mainly, though, I recommend the TK705STi for gamers who don’t need high-end home-cinema picture quality, since the overall performance of this projector is just average.
insights.locator: Intro — 'That said, the TK705STi is not for everyone'

insights.claim: Home cinema projector performance tracks price closely — high-end cineplex-mimicking models can cost upwards of $6,000 while sub-$1,000 units sacrifice brightness, contrast, and color quality — with the TK705STi sitting in the middle band.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: A simple price-tier map for the projector market that sets expectations for where margin and differentiation live.
insights.quote: High-end projectors that mimic what you see at the local cineplex can cost upwards of $6,000.
insights.locator: Opening — 'Home cinema projectors are all over the map'

insights.claim: The TK705STi's 0.8:1 throw ratio lets it produce a 10-foot-wide image from about 8 feet away, which the reviewer says makes it operable in nearly any room — placement flexibility as the practical selling point.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Short-throw geometry removes the dedicated-room requirement, expanding the addressable market for large-screen displays beyond home-theater buyers.
insights.quote: The TK705STi has a throw ratio of .8:1, which means you divide the wall size by the short-throw percentage.

insights.claim: The projector's ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) delivered stellar responsiveness with both a gaming laptop and an Xbox Series X, with controller input feeling immediate at a 10-foot image size even at high graphics settings.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Validates that latency, not panel quality, is the spec that sells projectors to console gamers.
insights.quote: My controller nudges felt immediate, and the entire game flowed with precision, as if I were on a gaming laptop screen instead.

insights.claim: The unit hits 98 percent of the older Rec. 709 color standard with no data on the current BT.2020 scale, lacks a 120-Hz refresh rate and VRR, and omits digital optical and Ethernet ports — spec gaps that mark it as deliberately not competing at the high end.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: The BT.2020 and VRR omissions are the concrete checklist items that separate midrange from premium — useful for judging competing spec sheets.
insights.quote: This model hits 98 percent of the older Rec. 709 standard, but there’s no data on the current BT.2020 scale.
insights.locator: 'For color gamut, the TK705STi doesn’t try to compete with the big guns'

insights.claim: Contrast was the projector's core weakness: dark scenes in Awake, The Creator, and Tron: Ares all looked too dark, and raising brightness grayed out the image without adding shadow detail that a Hisense XR10 reveals.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Contrast, not resolution, remains the differentiator buyers actually perceive — a persistent argument for premium projector pricing.
insights.quote: Raising the brightness level only grayed out the movies, but didn’t add detail.

insights.claim: Daytime and lit-room viewing was poor, with content looking washed out or barely viewable — the reviewer could not make out faces during bright scenes in a film on Tubi.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Ambient-light performance is the practical constraint keeping projectors a supplementary rather than primary display purchase.
insights.quote: Daytime viewing was not outstanding. Movies and shows looked washed out at best, or not even that viewable in a few cases.

insights.claim: Auto-keystoning on the TK705STi was finicky at best and often mapped incorrectly to the wall or screen, retriggering whenever the shaky-legged unit was jostled — though BenQ reps said this is not normal and could relate to the test screen.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Automated setup features are still unreliable enough to be a returns/support cost driver in midrange consumer AV.
insights.quote: a feature I found to be finicky at best, often mapping incorrectly to the wall or screen
insights.locator: 'After I put the projector in its spot'

insights.claim: Google TV made setup intuitive and app loading quick — about 10 minutes to ready — but a known Google TV glitch where the QR code does not work forced manual entry of login credentials.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Platform standardization on Google TV shifts the UX quality (and its bugs) from the hardware maker to the OS vendor across the whole projector category.
insights.quote: there’s a known Google TV glitch where the QR code doesn’t work, so I had to manually enter my Google login information
insights.locator: 'I like when projectors use Google TV'
